title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Specialty appliance and machine cleaning
audience: Any home-service operator who sets prices or plans monthly revenue, including solo operators.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a home-service business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level an appliance cleaning business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of sales adds to profit. For a specialist appliance cleaner the figure helps you decide whether a membership tier pays for itself, whether to add a second van, and how many visits a month you need before a new area is worth serving. It is only as good as the costs and percentages that go into it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of visits in a month. They can include the vehicle loan or lease, registration (paid yearly, so divide it by twelve), insurance, phone and software, a storage share, and equipment finance. Variable costs move with each visit. They include cleaning products, pads, microfibre, bags and filters, fuel for the van, and card or payment fees on each sale. ANZ defines fixed and variable costs and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss (ANZ, 21 February 2025, modified 22 July 2025). Express variable cost as a percentage of sales in the same period, and check that percentage across at least three months.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. One minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin, the share of each dollar of sales left to cover fixed costs. Xero's glossary states the same method (Xero Australia, 23 July 2026). Use the variable percentage as a decimal, so 18 per cent becomes 0.18 and the contribution margin is 0.82.

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source and date. Compute the contribution margin, then divide fixed costs by it. Convert the result into a number of visits at your average visit price, and round up to whole visits, because a part visit does not cover costs on its own. The average visit price must be the price you actually charged after membership discounts and minimums. The vendor's member and non-member prices are advertised figures, so use your own average, and show the membership mix that produced it.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost. Confirm that the output is revenue and not profit. Write down the reconciled figure with its inputs, and drop the others. A figure that cannot be checked should not be used to set prices.

procedure: List every monthly cost and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average visit price, and round up to whole visits.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: A one-person specialist appliance cleaner. All figures are hypothetical, invented for this lesson and not market data: fixed costs of $2,400 AUD a month, variable costs of 18 per cent of sales, and an average visit price of $200 AUD (illustrative, after membership discounts and minimums).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many visits must the business complete each month to break even, and what should it check before setting prices?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.18, which is 0.82. Break-even revenue is $2,400 AUD divided by 0.82, which is $2,926.83 AUD a month. At $200 AUD a visit, that is 14.63 visits, so the business needs 15 visits to cover its costs. Each visit contributes $164.00 AUD ($200 AUD multiplied by 0.82) towards fixed costs. Before setting prices, check that the 18 per cent includes every product, pad and payment fee, that the $2,400 is a monthly figure, and that $200 is the average visit price actually charged after any membership discount.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months, split into fixed and variable

commonErrors.error: Mixing monthly and annual figures, such as yearly registration added to monthly costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales.
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Copying the vendor's member price as your average visit price. Gap: no sourced appliance cost, margin or visit-volume figure exists.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the average price you actually charge, after discounts, and record the mix that produced it.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check the tax treatment of costs with a registered tax agent or qualified accountant.

GST: the ATO says a business must register once its GST turnover reaches the threshold, which it states as $75,000 (ATO, last updated 14 September 2026). Once registered, GST is included in the selling price. Confirm your own position with a registered tax agent.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period throughout, and the average visit price you actually charge.
Gap: no sourced appliance cost, margin or visit-volume figure exists. Recalculate from your own records.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $2,400 AUD a month and variable costs are 18% of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same appliance cleaning business. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the client today
Skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel
